This is not conservatism about a risky default; it is the only reading that survives a shared
database. A schema value describes what its author knows about, and an application legitimately
shares a server with another application, a reporting view, an operator's own table and the job
queue's two tables ([`core-classes/queue-storage-is-a-table`](core-classes.md#core-classes-queue-storage-is-a-table)). A converger treating its own value
as the complete truth of the database would drop every one of those on the first run.

Dropping is therefore something someone **writes**, and it is `Destructive`. There is no `--prune`,
no `allowDrops` and no strict mode: the escape hatch is the SQL the plan already printed, in the same
`Core\Db::execute` that is where a statement a human wrote goes.

A report is a step the plan carries and never applies, which is what keeps `applySafe` usable at all:
every plan against a shared database holds reports, and a rule reading *every* step's grade would
refuse every plan ever computed against a real database. `applySafe` reads the grades of the steps it
would run. Reports are still counted, printed and given complete SQL: a report the plan did not show
would be worse than one it will not apply.

**Declined:**
- **Dropping what the schema value omits, behind a flag or a strict mode.** Such a flag is correct only
  when the application owns the entire database, so its use anywhere else is a data-loss bug.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/schema-plan`](core-classes.md#core-classes-schema-plan), [`core-classes/schema-converges`](core-classes.md#core-classes-schema-converges), [`core-classes/queue-storage-is-a-table`](core-classes.md#core-classes-queue-storage-is-a-table).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-schema-apply-capability"></a>

## Planning is an ordinary read, and applying takes `db.schema` under a member named for its risk

`rule:core-classes/schema-apply-capability`

Computing a plan is an ordinary read. It issues catalog queries through the connection a program
already holds, under the `db.connect` it already has, and nothing about it is privileged.

Applying is not. It takes the deny-by-default `db.schema` capability
([`core-classes/db-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-capabilities)), which gates a different thing from `db.connect` and `db.open`:
not which database may be reached, but whether this program may issue DDL to it at all. It names
connection blocks, and an ungranted name throws naming the capability.

The two entry points are named for what they risk, at the call site. **`applySafe()`** refuses if any
step it would run is not `Safe`, and throws naming the first that is not.
**`applyIncludingRisky()`** says so where it is written, so a reviewer reading the call sees the
claim being made. `nvs schema plan|apply|dump` is the operator's spelling of the same thing.

**Declined:**
- **`applySafe` as the only entry point.** A tool that cannot express a risky change is a tool operators
  stop using, and they then hand-write the risky change with no grade at all. Naming the risk at the call
  site is stronger than refusing to have one.
- **One apply member with a `{risky: true}` option.** The option hides the claim inside an anonymous
  object, where the member's name puts it in front of the reviewer.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/db-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-capabilities), [`core-classes/schema-plan`](core-classes.md#core-classes-schema-plan), [`core-classes/queue-storage-is-a-table`](core-classes.md#core-classes-queue-storage-is-a-table).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-derive-attribute"></a>

## One written attribute per format generates a codec, and it is matched by resolved name

`rule:core-classes/derive-attribute`

A codec is generated only where a class asks for one, with one attribute per format: `#[Json\Derive]`
and `#[Db\Derive]` on the class, `#[Json\Field]` and `#[Db\Field]` on a property. The attribute makes
the class implement the corresponding interface; writing `implements Core\Json\Codec` beside it is
redundant but accepted.

**Opting in is answered at the call as well as at the declaration.** A member that builds an instance
out of a document or a row names the class in the call itself, so that is where the compiler asks
whether the class participates at all: one carrying neither the format's attribute nor the
hand-written half the derive would have generated — `fromJson` for a document, `fromRow` for a row —
is refused while compiling, `E0821` at a document door and `E0806` at a row's. Both doors answer the
same way, and both answer before the program runs, so a class no document could ever be read into is
not something the first request to reach the member discovers. The run-time refusal stays underneath
as the backstop for a descriptor built by hand, which no call site named.

**A compiler-recognized attribute is matched nominally.** The compiler acts on an attribute only when
its name *resolves*, through the ordinary namespace and `use` rules, to one of a closed `Core`-owned
list. So `#[Core\Json\Derive]` and a `use`d `#[Derive]` are one attribute reached two ways, while a
userland `type Derive = {};` is not it no matter how it is spelled, and a bare `#[{...}]` payload object
never triggers one because it resolves to no name at all. An import binds a whole short name and is
never a namespace prefix, so `use Core\Json;` followed by `#[Json\Derive]` names nothing.

This is a carve-out of exactly one sentence, and it is the only one: attribute *retrieval* stays
structural, unchanged ([`attributes/structural-retrieval`](attributes.md#attributes-structural-retrieval)). Every future compiler-recognized
attribute joins the closed list; nothing else is ever matched by name. The list itself is a single
table in the compiler (`nvs_types::derive::ATTRIBUTES`), and a rule adding an entry says its attribute
joins the list and states no running total, because a count restated beside each entry goes stale.

The nominal match is what lets the compiler generate code from an attribute at all: it acts on
**this** attribute, and never on a framework's own literal that happens to have the same shape. The
list is also the control on the attribute surface. Each entry is cheap to add, and a set of
attributes added because they were cheap is a second, undocumented language, so each entry is
argued on its own.

**Declined:**
- **Matching a compiler-recognized attribute structurally**, the way retrieval matches. The
  derive's payload is an empty shape, which structurally matches every attribute in a program, and
  even a non-empty one would generate code from a third-party literal that happens to fit.
- **One shared `#[Derive]` and `#[Field]` for both formats.** It forces a JSON key and a column
  name to be the same string, which is wrong often enough that two attributes would be needed at
  once. A class using both formats with the same rename writes it twice, and that is visible.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/derive-property-list`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-property-list), [`core-classes/derive-generates-what-is-missing`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-generates-what-is-missing), [`attributes/inert-metadata`](attributes.md#attributes-inert-metadata), [`attributes/structural-retrieval`](attributes.md#attributes-structural-retrieval).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-derive-property-list"></a>

## The field list is the declared property list, and every field is a constructor parameter of the same name

`rule:core-classes/derive-property-list`

Fields are the class's own declared properties, in declaration order, private ones included.
Visibility is an access-control decision and has no business deciding a wire format; declaration
order fixes encode order, so output is byte-deterministic across runs and machines.

**Every non-skipped field must also be a constructor parameter of the same name and type**, or the
derive is a compile error at the attribute. For a class written with promoted parameters the two
lists are literally the same declaration, so this costs nothing. It is worth its cost because a
decode is an ordinary `new`: the generated decoder fills locals and calls the constructor, so a
decoded object is indistinguishable from a hand-built one and every invariant the constructor
establishes still holds. A deriving class with no written `constructor` is therefore one compile
error at the attribute (`E0460`), even when every property carries a default: with no parameter
list, no field has a position to arrive through. A `lateinit` property cannot be a field, being by definition not
constructor-assigned; `readonly` is unaffected, because the constructor assigns it like any other.
Because the two lists are checked to agree at compile time, `fromJson(toJson($x))` rebuilding `$x`
is a property of the mechanism rather than of the care taken writing two functions, and a renamed
property breaks loudly: every reader of the old key gets a missing-field issue with its path.

A field's type must be codec-reachable — a scalar, one of the named `Core` value types, an enum, an
inline shape, an `array<T>` or `?T` of one of those, or another class that itself has a codec.
Anything else is a compile error at the field. Recursion is fine and terminates on the data, and it
is the *type* that recurses rather than only the field: an `array<T>` whose `T` is itself an
`array<…>` or an inline shape is reachable, and a decode reads every level of it. A row is the one
narrower door, because a column is a single value: [`core-classes/db-column-types`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-column-types) maps none to a
nested document, so `#[Db\Derive]` refuses a list of lists and a list of shapes at the declaration.

Two per-field overrides exist and no more: `name` renames one key or column, and `skip: true` removes
the field from the codec entirely. A property's overrides for one format are one attribute, so a second
`#[Json\Field]` or `#[Db\Field]` on it is a compile error at the second, naming the first: merging the
two would let one option silently win. A skipped property is exempt from the constructor-parameter rule
above, and a class keeping it as a parameter anyway stays well formed — it still encodes, and the
program can still build one itself. What such a class cannot do is be **decoded**: the contract names
no key for that position, and a default carried on a field cannot be read for a position that has no
field. So the refusal is of the call that asks for a whole instance out of a document or a row rather
than of the declaration, at every door that reads a derived codec. A field's default key or column
is the property's own name, exactly, with no case mapping between the two.

**The key is the field's identity**, so two fields of one format with equal keys are a compile error
at the second (`E0873`), naming the first. The encoder would write the key twice, and the decoder
would fill both properties from one value. A JSON decode reads a class only from a JSON object and
an `array<T>` only from a JSON list: `["a"]` and `{"0": "a"}` have the same entries once read, and
the decode tells them apart by what the document wrote.

**Declined:**
- **Building the object without its constructor**, the way a serializer for a language with no
  constructors does. Every decoded object would be one that never ran its class's invariants, and
  the deliberately narrow reflection bypass of [`classes/an-unwritten-property-read-throws`](classes.md#classes-an-unwritten-property-read-throws)
  would become a hot path.
- **Deriving from the constructor's parameters alone.** The encoder has nothing to read for a
  parameter that is not promoted, and the two halves would come from two lists that can disagree
  in silence, which is the failure hand-written codecs already have.
- **A whole-class naming policy** such as `snake_case`. It is a mode string
  ([`core-api/shape-rules`](core-api.md#core-api-shape-rules) R11), and it makes a wire format depend on a setting rather than on
  the source being read.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`core-classes/derive-reports-every-field`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-reports-every-field), [`core-classes/db-column-types`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-column-types).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-keep-key-order-freezes-a-derived-classs-keys"></a>

## `#[Core\Json\KeepKeyOrder]` freezes a derived class's JSON key order, and compiles only beside `#[Core\Json\Derive]`

`rule:core-classes/keep-key-order-freezes-a-derived-classs-keys`

`#[Core\Json\KeepKeyOrder(reason: string)]` is a compiler-recognized attribute
([`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute)'s closed list), allowed on a class only, with one required field,
`reason`. It says the class's JSON key order is read by somebody: a consumer that wants a `type` key
first, an ETag, a signed or cached document.

**It compiles only on a class that also carries `#[Core\Json\Derive]`.** Anywhere else it would do
nothing, so it is a compile error at the attribute, naming the missing derive. The codec itself does
nothing new with it: the encode order is the declaration order
([`core-classes/derive-property-list`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-property-list)), as it always is.

**What it freezes is the order the tools write** ([`tooling/class-members-have-one-order`](tooling.md#tooling-class-members-have-one-order)). A
derived class's field order is its instance properties in written order, with the promoted constructor
parameters at the constructor's position. Under `KeepKeyOrder`, the instance properties keep their
written order, and every other member of the class is ordered as usual. The ordered layout puts the
constructor after every property, so when a promoted parameter comes before a declared property in the
field order, no member order keeps it: the class is then left exactly as written, and `nvs code order`
prints one note naming it.

An empty `reason` compiles. Review judges a reason, and a check cannot.

It is named for JSON because `Core\Json\Derive` is the only derived codec whose output order a consumer
reads: `Core\Db\Derive` matches columns by name.

**Declined:**
- **A generic `KeepOrder`.** The compiler could not check that it sits where an order means something.
- **An `order` field on `Core\Json\Field`.** It is a second way to write the order the declaration
  already gives.
- **Refusing an empty `reason`.** Review judges a reason, and a check cannot.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`core-classes/derive-property-list`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-property-list), [`tooling/class-members-have-one-order`](tooling.md#tooling-class-members-have-one-order).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-derive-reports-every-field"></a>

## A generated decoder reports every failed field at once, before the constructor runs

`rule:core-classes/derive-reports-every-field`

A generated decoder does not stop at the first bad field. It decodes every field, **accumulating
issues**, and if any were recorded it throws once, before the constructor is called, so no half-built
object exists.

An issue is `{path: string, message: string}`, and `path` is a dotted path into the payload —
`"address.city"`, `"tags.3"` — so a nested class's issues arrive at the top-level `catch` already
located. For a row decode it is the column name. `ParseError` carries the list; no new exception
class was added for it, because `ParseError` is already exactly the right node: *input did not match
a format this code declared*.

A whole list is the point: a submitted form has to tell its user about every bad field at once, not
one per round trip.

`Core\Db\DbError` has no `issues` slot, because it sits outside the exception tree whose classes carry
one, so the row half's per-field refusals are reported on a `ParseError`, the class `decodeAs` throws
for the same question. `crates/nvs-stdlib/src/db/mod.rs`'s module doc owns why.

- **Memory:** the accumulator is allocated only when the first issue is recorded, so the successful
  path — every request that is not an error — allocates nothing for it.

**Declined:**
- **Reporting the first failed field only.** It suits a configuration file and fails a form, whose
  user would be told about one mistake at a time.
- **A new exception class per format.** The closed `Throwable` set exists so that `catch` is
  learnable ([`errors/throwable-hierarchy`](errors.md#errors-throwable-hierarchy)), and what was missing was a field on an existing
  class, not a new class.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/derive-property-list`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-property-list), [`core-classes/db-error`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-error), [`errors/throwable-hierarchy`](errors.md#errors-throwable-hierarchy).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-derive-generates-what-is-missing"></a>

## The derive generates only the half the class does not write, at compile time, storing nothing per object

`rule:core-classes/derive-generates-what-is-missing`

The derive generates only what the class does not declare itself. A class writing its own encoder and
carrying the attribute gets the generated decoder and keeps its encoder — the common real case, since
a custom representation usually needs a mechanical inverse rather than a second bespoke one. A class
declaring **both** halves is a compile error: the attribute would generate nothing, and an attribute
with no effect is a mistake rather than a no-op.

`#[Db\Derive]` is one-directional. The row codec declares a read only; a write is an explicit
statement plus bound parameters, and generating an `INSERT` is the ORM already settled against. The
graph-copy operation gets no derive either: it handles every object with no per-class opt-in and is
not a declared wire contract at all. An anonymous object encodes with no attribute, because an
anonymous object has no declaration to carry one and no identity a property list could only guess at — its
encoding is structural, keyed on its field names alone. And there is **no validation**: a derived
codec checks types and presence, not that an email looks like one.

What it costs: a compile-time pass over the classes carrying the attribute, recording each one's field
list on its class descriptor for both halves to walk, field by field. **Nothing is stored per object**,
and the only question either half asks at run time is whether the class wrote the half being read —
one lookup in the method table the walk is already holding, taken once per instance rather than once
per field, and paid on the encoding side by a refcount pair per level of the document while that
member runs. Footprint is O(derived classes in compiled code), not O(objects) and not O(requests), and
a program that neither carries the attribute nor writes a half pays nothing at all, including no pass.

**Declined:**
- **Hand-written codecs only.** A ten-property class costs twenty lines per format that restate the
  property list above them, and an encoder and a decoder that drift apart fail in silence.
- **Encoding every public property with no attribute.** A class's public shape would be a wire
  contract nobody wrote ([`core-api/written-participation`](core-api.md#core-api-written-participation)).
- **A derive for the graph copy.** It already handles every object with no opt-in, so a derive would
  be a second path to an operation that works ([`classes/two-copy-depths`](classes.md#classes-two-copy-depths)).
- **Validation in the codec.** Checking that a value looks right belongs to `Core\Validate` and user
  code, and folding it in is how a derive attribute grows into a framework.
- **Omitting a `null` field and a naming policy** are declined where their rules live
  ([`core-api/required-optional-and-nullable`](core-api.md#core-api-required-optional-and-nullable), [`core-classes/derive-property-list`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-property-list)). Until either
  exists, a payload that needs one takes a hand-written encoder.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`core-classes/derive-property-list`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-property-list), [`types/anonymous-object`](types.md#types-anonymous-object), [`types/shape-type`](types.md#types-shape-type).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ldap-capabilities"></a>

## Three deny-by-default capabilities gate naming an LDAP block, dialling a directory, and binding without TLS, and nothing is read from `ldap.conf` or the environment

`rule:core-classes/ldap-capabilities`

Three deny-by-default capabilities under `[capabilities.ldap]` sit in front of a directory, in `db.*`'s shape. `ldap.connect` names the `[ldap.<name>]` blocks a program may open with `Ldap::connect`; `ldap.open` names the hosts an `Ldap\Settings` may reach with `Ldap::open`, and takes `*.` at a label boundary; `ldap.cleartext` names the hosts a bind may reach without TLS ([`security/ldap-cleartext-bind-is-granted-per-host`](security.md#security-ldap-cleartext-bind-is-granted-per-host)).

A block's address is the operator's, so a `connect`-named block is pre-approved and is not checked
against the outbound address policy, as [`core-classes/db-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-capabilities) reasons for a database. An
`open` target is the program's: its host is checked against `ldap.open` and its address against
[`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy) in full before anything is dialled.

`[ldap.<name>]` follows `[db.<name>]`: `url` (one `ldaps://` or `ldap://` URL, or a list), `base`,
`user`, `password` or `password_file` ([`config/a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value`](config.md#config-a-secret-is-a-file-whose-content-is-the-value)),
`tls` (`"required"`, the default, or `"none"`), `tls_ca_file`, `timeout` and `pool`, and every table
refuses an unknown key. A block with no `user` binds anonymously. `Ldap\Settings` is the same fields as
a shape: `url` is a sink with no launderer, as `Settings.host` is for a database; `base` is
`Dn|string`; `user` accepts `tainted`, being a length-framed protocol field; `password` is `secret
tainted string`; and `tls` is the enum `Ldap::Tls`.

**A block's URL list fails over in order**, and so does every address one URL's host resolves to. A
server that does not answer, or whose TLS handshake fails, moves the walk on. A server that answers and
refuses the credentials stops it, because the next server would refuse them too and the walk would
only add to the account's lockout count.

A timeout has a default and no spelling for unlimited. Nothing is read from `ldap.conf`, `LDAPTLS_*` or
any other environment, so no setting one request's code makes can reach another request's connection,
and TLS trust is relaxed only where [`security/tls-trust-is-relaxed-only-under-a-host-grant`](security.md#security-tls-trust-is-relaxed-only-under-a-host-grant)
already allows it per host.

**Declined:**
- **A binding to OpenLDAP's `libldap`.** It brings process-wide options, a second TLS stack beside the
  one [`security/one-tls-client`](security.md#security-one-tls-client) allows, `ldap.conf` and the environment, and SASL through
  `libsasl2`, and a TLS option set for one connection can then apply to the next request's.
- **A tokio-based client crate.** It needs a second scheduler per core, which
  [`concurrency/one-scheduler`](concurrency.md#concurrency-one-scheduler) refuses; the BER codec is borrowed sans-IO and the sequencing is
  written over the runtime's own TCP and TLS streams ([`core-classes/db-crate-boundary`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-crate-boundary)).
- **An unlimited timeout, and reading `ldap.conf` or `LDAPTLS_*`.** Both put a connection's behaviour
  outside what the operator's configuration states.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/db-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-capabilities), [`security/ldap-cleartext-bind-is-granted-per-host`](security.md#security-ldap-cleartext-bind-is-granted-per-host), [`security/ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block`](security.md#security-ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ldap-search-pages-and-never-follows-a-referral"></a>

## An LDAP search reads one page at a time, throws at a server limit and never follows a referral, and every control is a named option

`rule:core-classes/ldap-search-pages-and-never-follows-a-referral`

`Ldap\Connection::search` returns an `Ldap\Entries` that reads one page at a time as the loop reaches it, throws when the server stopped at a size or time limit, and never follows a referral. Every control `Core\Ldap` sends is a named option of the member it changes, and every extended operation is the member that needs it.

`search` sends the paged-results control (RFC 2696) on every request, `pageSize` 1000 by default, and
reads the first page itself, so a base that does not exist or a filter the server refuses throws at the
call. **A size or time limit the server hit throws** `SizeLimitExceeded` or `TimeLimitExceeded`, and
the page it came with is dropped, so a partial result is never returned as if it were complete. A
connection released with a search still paging is closed, not pooled
([`security/ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block`](security.md#security-ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block)). `read` is a base-scope search for one entry and
returns `null` for `noSuchObject`.

**A referral is never followed.** A continuation reference in a search is data, read from
`Entries::references()`; a referral answering any other operation throws the kind `Referral`. A
referral the client followed would dial a server the server named, not one the operator or a grant in
[`core-classes/ldap-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-capabilities) named.

Active Directory's four extras are named options or members:

- **Sort and a window.** `sort` (one attribute, because AD sorts on one key) with `descending`, and
  `window` with `offset`, which need `sort`, replace paging for that search, and fill
  `Entries::total()` with the server's count. Both are checked before anything is sent.
- **Deleted objects.** `showDeleted` includes deleted entries, and `Entry::isDeleted` says which.
- **Incremental sync.** `changes` is DirSync: it returns the entries changed since the `cookie` the
  program stored, and `Changes::cookie()` is the next one. On a server without DirSync it throws
  `Unsupported`.
- **The Global Catalog** is a block whose URL uses port 3268 or 3269. It is read-only: every write but
  `compare` throws `ReadOnly` before a byte is sent.

`modify` sends one Modify request, so the server applies every `Ldap\Change` in order or none of them.
`rename` derives the new first level and, where it moved, the new parent from its second DN. `compare`
returns `bool` and throws on an error.

- **Memory:** a search holds one page of up to `pageSize` entries and the current entry, per search a
  request has open. A finished search leaves nothing on its connection.

**Declined:**
- **A `bind` member, a raw-control member and a raw-extended-operation member.** Each would be a
  second form of an operation the named members already have
  ([`core-api/one-paradigm-per-operation`](core-api.md#core-api-one-paradigm-per-operation)), and a rebind would let a request change a pooled
  connection's identity.
- **Following referrals, or a rebind callback.** See above.
- **`uSNChanged` polling pinned to one controller.** It is a second form of DirSync's job, correct only
  while every call reaches the same controller, which the URL list's failover does not promise.
- **A client-side sort, as PHP's `ldap_sort`.** The server sorts with `sort`, so a second sort would be
  a second form of the same operation.
- **A `compare` that returns `-1` on an error.** A third value a caller has to test for beside `true`
  and `false`.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/ldap-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-capabilities), [`core-classes/ldap-filter-is-a-value`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-filter-is-a-value), [`core-classes/db-streaming`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-streaming).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ldap-filter-is-a-value"></a>

## An LDAP filter is an immutable value encoded straight to BER, whose values accept `tainted` and whose attribute names are a sink

`rule:core-classes/ldap-filter-is-a-value`

An LDAP filter is an immutable `Ldap\Filter` value, encoded straight to BER, whose values are data and whose attribute names are a sink. It is made by static functions — `equals`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `contains`, `present`, `atLeast`, `atMost`, `approx` — and combined with `all`, `any` and `not`; there is no fluent chain, and no `<` or `>` because RFC 4511 has none. Base, scope, attributes and paging are search options, never part of the filter.

**The split follows [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate).** A filter on the wire is a BER structure, not
text, so a value is a framed octet string the server compares against and never parses: it accepts
`tainted`, and `*)(objectClass=*` or a NUL byte matches only itself. An attribute name selects what the
server evaluates, so it is a sink, checked against RFC 4512's attribute-description grammar, and
anything else throws `LogicError`. A value may be a string, bytes, an `int`, a `bool`, a `Core\Uuid`, an
`Ldap\Sid` or an `Instant`, encoded at search time by the table [`core-classes/ldap-value-types`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-value-types)
reads with, so a GUID filter matches the server's byte order.

**The names `Connection::add` writes are the same sink, and they arrive as an array's keys.** A
parameter cannot mark a key, so the call itself refuses a key that can come from outside the program:
a literal's key that is not a literal, a constant or a plain variable, a spread, and any other array
whose keys a visitor could have chosen ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)). The values stay data and
accept `tainted`. Without the refusal, a form posted as an array could add `objectClass` or
`userAccountControl` within whatever the bind account may write.

**No filter escaper exists.** The builder is the protocol's own shape, the way a bound parameter is
SQL's, so an escaper would be a second, weaker answer. [`core-classes/db-one-api`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-one-api) keeps query
builders out of `Core` because SQL has a text form the server executes; LDAP has none on the wire, and
that rule is about SQL. `Filter::parse` reads RFC 4515 text an operator wrote, and its parameter refuses
`tainted`. `toString` renders that text for a log and is itself `tainted`. `Ldap\Ad` adds AD's matching
rules as filters: `memberOf` with `nested: true` (`1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941`), `bitAnd` and `bitOr`
(`.803`, `.804`), `enabled` and `disabled`.

**A filter nests at most 100 levels of `all`, `any` and `not`.** Reading and writing a filter recurse
once per level, so a filter a request built in a loop would otherwise exhaust the thread's stack and
take every request on the core down with it. The builder that would pass the limit throws
`LogicError`, and so does `parse` at the `(` that does; no filter a person writes comes near it.

**Declined:**
- **`Filter::escape` beside text filters.** A second, weaker answer to a question the value builder
  settles, and an escaper over filter text is the catch-all [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named)
  forbids.
- **A fluent filter chain.** `->and()` beside `all` would be two ways to write the same tree, and a
  chain's order is something a reader has to simulate.
- **Leaving filters and AD's types to a package.** A package cannot be a launderer
  ([`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named)), and a GUID read in the wrong byte order is a bug every
  caller would write once.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/ldap-dn-is-the-launderer`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-dn-is-the-launderer), [`core-classes/ldap-value-types`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-value-types), [`core-classes/db-one-api`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-one-api), [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ldap-dn-is-the-launderer"></a>

## `Ldap\Dn` is the one launderer for the DN sink, and every DN parameter takes a `Dn` or a string that refuses `tainted`

`rule:core-classes/ldap-dn-is-the-launderer`

`Ldap\Dn` is the one launderer for the DN sink: it is built from an attribute type and a value that may be `tainted`, and escapes the value per RFC 4514. A DN is parsed by the server into a path in the directory tree, so a DN parameter is an instruction by [`security/sink-predicate`](security.md#security-sink-predicate), and [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named) puts its launderer in `Core`.

`Dn::of` and `$dn->child` take the attribute type, checked against RFC 4512's grammar, and the value.
Every member that takes a DN takes `Dn|string`, and the `string` arm refuses `tainted`; `Dn::parse`
refuses it too, for text an operator wrote. The launderer returns a carrier, not a string
([`security/launderer-answers-a-carrier`](security.md#security-launderer-answers-a-carrier)), so a value laundered for a DN reaches only a DN
parameter. A DN the server returns comes back as a `Dn`, and `parent`, `rdnAttribute`, `rdnValue` and
`isWithin` read one without text handling. The first level is two readers rather than one returning
`{attribute, value}`, because a `Core` member cannot return a shape. Every text a `Dn` gives back,
`toString` and `rdnValue`, is `tainted`, since a value in it may be. There is no `ldap_escape`, and no
escaper for filter text either ([`core-classes/ldap-filter-is-a-value`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-filter-is-a-value)).

<sub>See also [`core-classes/ldap-filter-is-a-value`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-filter-is-a-value), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`security/launderer-answers-a-carrier`](security.md#security-launderer-answers-a-carrier).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ldap-value-types"></a>

## Each LDAP attribute has one natural type from the schema and a fixed table of Active Directory names, and a typed reader converts only where nothing is lost

`rule:core-classes/ldap-value-types`

Each LDAP attribute has one natural type, given by the server's schema plus a fixed table of Active Directory names, and a typed reader on `Ldap\Entry` converts only where nothing is lost. The principle is [`core-classes/db-column-types`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-column-types)'s: anything else throws, and text and bytes are `tainted`.

The schema gives the base type — AD's `attributeSyntax`/`oMSyntax`, or the subschema's `SYNTAX` OID on
any other server — read lazily, once per pool, and immutable after. The fixed table gives what the
schema cannot say:

| Attribute | Natural type |
|---|---|
| `objectGUID` and every GUID-valued AD attribute | `Core\Uuid`, the first three groups byte-swapped from AD's mixed-endian form |
| `objectSid`, `tokenGroups`, `sIDHistory` | `Ldap\Sid` (`S-1-5-21-…`) |
| FILETIME integers (`pwdLastSet`, `lastLogonTimestamp`, `accountExpires`, `lockoutTime`, …) | `?Instant`; `0` and `0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` are `null` |
| negative intervals (`maxPwdAge`, `lockoutDuration`, …) | `Duration` |
| GeneralizedTime | `Instant` |
| `TRUE`/`FALSE` | `bool` |
| `userAccountControl` with `msDS-User-Account-Control-Computed` | `Ad\AccountFlags` |
| `groupType` | `Ad\GroupType` |
| `sAMAccountType` | the enum `Entry::AccountType` |

**A flag field is a readonly object with one `bool` reader method per flag** and an immutable `with`
taking one `bool` option per flag it may set, where an option left out keeps its bit; `Core` has no
general flag-set type. Bits the object does not name are kept, so a write never drops them. Lockout and
an expired password are read from the computed attribute, and `mustChangePassword` from `pwdLastSet =
0`, both of which `search` requests whenever `userAccountControl` is selected, because AD does not
store them in `userAccountControl`, and a reader of the stored attribute alone would report a locked
account as active; `with` cannot set them. A value is written in the form it is read, so every type above round-trips through
`modify` and is encoded the same way inside a filter. A ranged attribute (`member;range=0-1499`) is
fetched to its end and returned whole under its plain name. An attribute name matches without case and
keeps the server's case.

- **Memory:** the schema is one map per block per core, O(blocks) and not O(requests). A merged ranged
  attribute is the whole list, and counts against the request's memory cap like any other value.

**Declined:**
- **A general bit-flag type in `Core`.** Three AD fields need it; a readonly object per field names
  every flag and costs nothing anywhere else.
- **An array with a `count` key and lowercased attribute names, as PHP's `ldap_get_entries` returns.**
  The typed readers replace it, and `toArray` keeps the server's spelling.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/db-column-types`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-column-types), [`core-classes/ldap-filter-is-a-value`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ldap-filter-is-a-value).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ldap-error"></a>

## Every `Core\Ldap` failure is one `Ldap\LdapError` with a kind to branch on and the LDAP result code, and no message carries a password

`rule:core-classes/ldap-error`

Every failure the directory or the wire reports is one class, `Ldap\LdapError`, with `$kind`, an `Ldap\LdapError::Kind` a program branches on, and `$code`, the LDAP result code, or `null` where no server sent one. A malformed attribute name, DN or URL is the program's own `LogicError` or `RuntimeError`, and a pool with no free slot is an `IOError`, as for `Core\Db`.

The kinds are `InvalidCredentials`, `AccountDisabled` (AD `data 533`), `AccountLocked` (775),
`PasswordExpired` (532), `MustChangePassword` (773), `AccountExpired` (701), `NotAllowedNow` (530,
531), `EncryptionRequired`, `PasswordPolicy`, `NoSuchObject`, `AlreadyExists`, `InsufficientAccess`,
`ConstraintViolation`, `SizeLimitExceeded`, `TimeLimitExceeded`, `Referral`, `ReadOnly`,
`Unsupported`, `Unavailable`, `Timeout` and `Protocol`. One class with a kind lets a program branch on
the condition rather than on a result code, for the reason [`core-classes/db-error`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-error) gives
`Core\Db\DbError`.

An unknown user (525) and a wrong password (52e) are both `InvalidCredentials`
([`security/ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block`](security.md#security-ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block)). AD's policy refusal of a new password is
`PasswordPolicy`. **No message carries a password or a value of a filter**: a message is built from
the operation's name, the result code and the server's own diagnostic.

**Declined:**
- **`false` and a separate error number, as PHP's `ldap_errno` gives.** A failure throws, so a
  caller that forgets to test a return value cannot read a failure as a result.
- **Distinct kinds for 525 and 52e.** A user-enumeration oracle handed to every login form.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/db-error`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-error), [`security/ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block`](security.md#security-ldap-pool-is-bound-as-its-block).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-queue-storage-is-a-table"></a>

## The job queue is two tables in a connection the operator names, converged by an explicit command

`rule:core-classes/queue-storage-is-a-table`

Durable background jobs live in one jobs table and one dead-letter table, in a connection the
operator names in `[queue]`. The runtime owns that schema **as a value** — a `Core\Db\Schema`
converged by `nvs queue migrate`, an explicit operator command — which is one description of the two
tables rather than one per dialect. A hand-written DDL list per backend is one chance to drift per
backend, and the backend nobody wrote is indistinguishable from one nobody supports.

**At most one *pending* job per dedupe key, and what enforces it is a plain column under a plain
unique key.** The jobs table carries `dedupe_pending`, which the statements maintain: it holds the
job's `dedupe_key` while the job is pending and `null` once it is claimed, succeeded, cancelled or
dead-lettered. A partial index (`… where state = 0`) and a stored generated column each say the same
thing, and neither is in [`core-classes/schema-is-a-value`](core-classes.md#core-classes-schema-is-a-value)'s vocabulary — they are two dialects'
answers to one requirement, which is exactly what a schema value exists to stop being. A null
collides with nothing on any of the five, because a unique key's nulls are distinct on every backend
([`core-classes/a-unique-key-reads-nulls-as-distinct`](core-classes.md#core-classes-a-unique-key-reads-nulls-as-distinct)) — four give it directly and SQL Server
through the filtered index its emitter writes — so the guarantee is one guarantee, stated once, on
every backend `Core\Queue` runs a statement against.

That is the queue reading a property of the vocabulary rather than the queue asking for one. The
alternative — a `not null` column with a generated token per released row — is refused for a reason
that outlives any one backend: such a column cannot be added to a table that already holds rows, so
it would be a schema no existing deployment could converge to, while a nullable one arrives as a
`Safe` step.

DDL is an injection sink and a privileged act, so **the runtime never issues it implicitly**, not at
boot and not from a request; applying the plan takes `db.schema` like any other DDL
([`core-classes/schema-apply-capability`](core-classes.md#core-classes-schema-apply-capability)). A server whose queue database is behind that schema
does not create what is missing: it refuses to serve and names `nvs queue migrate`. That makes the
migrate command one more operator step a deployment has to get right, and implicit DDL from a running
server is worse in every way that matters here.

It may be the application's own database, and that is the recommended configuration, because a
transactional enqueue — the property the whole design rests on — requires it. A separate queue
database is permitted and silently gives up that property, which is why the documentation says so at
the point the option is offered. The cost of the recommended configuration is write load on the
application's primary database, and that cost is the reason `[queue] connection` is a setting at all.

**Declined:**
- **A runtime-owned durable log on disk.** It ties a job to one machine's disk, so a second instance
  cannot see it and a rescheduled container loses it, and durability becomes the runtime's to prove
  rather than the database's to provide.
- **`Core\Cache` as the store.** It must always be correct to find nothing in the cross-request store
  ([`concurrency/cross-request-state-is-explicit`](concurrency.md#concurrency-cross-request-state-is-explicit)), which is right for a cache and disqualifying
  for a job somebody is waiting on.
- **Creating the tables at boot or on first use.** DDL is a privileged act an operator takes, never one
  a running server takes on its own.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/schema-converges`](core-classes.md#core-classes-schema-converges), [`core-classes/schema-apply-capability`](core-classes.md#core-classes-schema-apply-capability), [`core-classes/db-capabilities`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-capabilities).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly"></a>

## A session is opened by calling `Core\Session::start`, and there is no ambient session array

`rule:core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`

There is no ambient session array and no implicit session start. A script calls `Core\Session::start`
— or an equivalent resuming a presented identifier — before reading or writing session state, so
"this request uses sessions" is a line in the source rather than a fact discoverable only by grepping
for a superglobal. A member called before `start` throws naming itself, and the refusal is catchable
at the root like any other.

The shape is fixed here: a class, an explicit start, no ambient array. The mechanics are a feature of
their own — the store is the shared cache tier or the database, the memory tier is refused at boot
because a session held by one process is not a session, there is no lock, and expiry is the store's
own rather than a sweeper's.

What this costs is one line per request that uses sessions. What it buys is that a request that does
not use them pays nothing, which the ambient version could never promise.

**Starting is not storing.** A `start` for a visitor with no session opens an empty one with no
identifier: no row is written and no cookie is sent. The first write that leaves something in it
draws the identifier and sends the cookie, and the end of the request writes the row. So the store
grows with sessions somebody wrote, never with requests served, and a flood of cookieless requests
that only read leaves nothing behind. `regenerate` on such a session does nothing, because no client
holds an identifier for it, and `destroy` has no row to delete.

**A CSRF token counts as a write.** `Core\Csrf::token` binds its token to the identifier the response
sends, so on a session with none it draws one and sends the cookie, and it marks the session changed
even while the record is empty, so the end of the request writes the row and the next request's
`start` finds it. It spends one row per visitor who is shown a token, and `[session] ttl` expires it.

**Declined:**
- **A session that starts on the first `Core\Session` access.** A read that starts a session is a side
  effect at a distance, the kind of hidden step the explicit `start` exists to remove.

<sub>See also [`statements/no-host-populated-variables`](statements.md#statements-no-host-populated-variables), [`core-classes/cli-arguments`](core-classes.md#core-classes-cli-arguments), [`core-classes/script-args`](core-classes.md#core-classes-script-args).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ratelimit-two-members"></a>

## `consume` and `shed` are two jobs with two verbs, and neither is a tier of the other

`rule:core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`

`Core\RateLimit::consume` and `::shed` are two jobs with two verbs, and the verb says which one you
are doing. `consume` enforces a policy the application promised somebody — a plan quota, a login
limit — over the shared store, coherently, because a policy only approximately enforced is not
enforced. `shed` drops load to keep a host up, from the serving process's own memory, and an
approximate answer is entirely adequate for that because the goal is "less than the amount that
hurts", not a number. `shed`'s contract states its arithmetic out loud: its count is per server
process, so a limit of 100 on each of four processes admits up to 400 across the deployment, and an
arrival the cache's cap forgets admits a burst again.

`shed` keeps its count in the memory tier ([`concurrency/the-memory-tier-is-one-store-per-process`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-memory-tier-is-one-store-per-process)),
scoped by app and configuration generation like any key there and bounded by the same
`[cache.memory] max_size`. The read and the write of one arrival are one step under the shard's write
lock, so every core of a process charges the same count and two cores never both admit the last unit.

They are not two tiers of one operation, and a flag on one member could not carry the difference.

The class exists for the limits only the application can key: five failed logins per *account*, a
quota per tenant plan, ten exports per user per hour. Per-account login throttling is what stops
credential stuffing, which per-IP throttling does not, because the attacker has many addresses and
the victim has one account — and no proxy knows which account a request authenticates as. Left
without a class, an application writes one of two wrong limiters: a counter kept with `get` and `put`
in the memory tier, which two cores race and every process counts on its own, or an insert-and-count
against the database, which puts a write on the hot path of the endpoint it protects. The price of `consume`'s coherence is a network
round trip on that path, the same floor the shared cache tier accepts, and it is why `shed` exists
for the cases that do not need it.

Four things are deliberately absent. **Edge and flood limiting** — no per-IP, per-path or connection
limit as a deployment feature: a proxy owns it earlier and cheaper, and doing it here means paying
for the request in order to reject it. **All configuration** — a limit is application policy, so
there is no `[ratelimit]` block at all. **Any automatic enforcement** — the member returns a decision
and writes no `429`. **Distributed reservation** and multi-key atomic checks, which are considerably
more machinery with no named use case yet.

**Declined:**
- **Only the shared tier.** The two names work only if both exist. With one, the first program that
  needs approximate load shedding uses `consume` for it, and puts a round trip on a path that did not
  need one.
- **One member with a `coherent: true` option.** The default is chosen once and copied, and the wrong
  choice fails silently — the reason `Core\Cache` has two members
  ([`core-api/two-cache-tiers`](core-api.md#core-api-two-cache-tiers)).

- **A middleware or attribute that applies a limit to a route.** It needs a dispatch pipeline Novis
  does not have ([`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered)), and what to do about a limit is
  application logic.
- **Backing it with `Core\Db`.** It puts a write on the hot path of every protected endpoint, on the
  database that is usually the scarcest resource in the deployment.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/ratelimit-gcra`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-gcra), [`core-classes/ratelimit-unreachable-store-throws`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-unreachable-store-throws), [`core-classes/topic`](core-classes.md#core-classes-topic).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ratelimit-gcra"></a>

## Both tiers run GCRA over one stored timestamp per key, and the `Decision` computes `retryAfter`

`rule:core-classes/ratelimit-gcra`

Both members implement the **generic cell rate algorithm** — a leaky bucket expressed as one stored
timestamp, the theoretical arrival time of the next permitted request. `limit` per `per` sets the
drain rate, `burst` (defaulting to `limit`) sets how much may arrive at once, and `cost` weights one
call so an expensive endpoint may consume five units of the same quota.

One duration of arithmetic per call, and **one stored timestamp per key** rather than a window of
them. In the shared store that is the difference between O(1) and O(requests in window) memory per
key, which is what makes limiting per user affordable at a million users. `retryAfter` is computed
rather than estimated, where a sliding-window counter can only answer "sometime in the next window" —
the answer that makes clients retry in a burst at the window edge. Both tiers run the identical
algorithm, so moving a call between them changes the *guarantee* and not the shape of the answer.

The `Decision` is readonly `allowed`, `limit`, `remaining` and `retryAfter`, the last being `?Duration`
and `null` exactly when `allowed` is true — absence is `?T`, not a sentinel zero. Both members are
qualifier-neutral. The key **accepts `tainted`**, since a tenant or account id is user-derived by
nature and the store's protocol is length-prefixed, so a key cannot reshape a command; it
**refuses `secret`**, because using a signing key as a rate-limit key writes it into a store with a
TTL. A program that needs to limit on a secret keys on a hash of it (`Core\Hash::of`). `shed`'s
half is one step over a timestamp in the memory tier; `consume`'s is a small script of our own in
the shared store, an algorithm over our own state.

**Declined:**
- **A sliding-window counter or log.** The counter cannot give an exact `retryAfter`, and the log
  holds O(requests in window) per key in a store somebody pays for.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-two-members), [`core-classes/ratelimit-unreachable-store-throws`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-unreachable-store-throws), [`core-classes/secret-reveal`](core-classes.md#core-classes-secret-reveal), [`types/duration`](types.md#types-duration).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-ratelimit-unreachable-store-throws"></a>

## An unreachable shared store throws, because whether to fail open is knowledge only the call site has

`rule:core-classes/ratelimit-unreachable-store-throws`

`consume` on an unreachable shared store throws. It does **not** return `allowed: true`.

This is the load-bearing choice. A security control that fails open silently is worse than no
control, because the deployment believes it has one — and whether *this* limiter should fail open or
closed is knowledge only the call site has. A login throttle must fail closed; a plan quota should
fail open rather than take the product down. Throwing puts the decision where the knowledge is, and
an application that chooses to fail open does so in a `catch` that a reader can see and a reviewer
can question.

`shed` cannot fail this way, its state being in the serving process's own memory, which is one more reason the
two are different members rather than one with a flag.

**Declined:**
- **Failing open**, returning `allowed: true` with a logged warning. A security control that has
  stopped working would look like one that is working.
- **Failing closed**, returning `allowed: false`. A store outage would take the whole application
  down, and a quota check is not worth that.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-two-members), [`core-classes/ratelimit-gcra`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-gcra), [`errors/propagation`](errors.md#errors-propagation).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-crypto-interop-tier"></a>

## `Core\Crypto`'s algorithm roster is closed, every algorithm argument is required, and the sealed layout is what a browser reads

`rule:core-classes/crypto-interop-tier`

`Core\Crypto`'s algorithm roster is closed, every algorithm argument is required, and no member name
carries an algorithm.

The roster is AES-256-GCM beside XChaCha20-Poly1305, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, HKDF-SHA256, ECDH over P-256
and X25519, and four signature algorithms — RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and RSASSA-PSS over SHA-256, ECDSA over
P-256, and Ed25519. AES Key Wrap and the Concat KDF are internal to PBES2 and ECDH-ES and never members.
Out, permanently: AES-CBC, AES-CTR, AES-128, RSA encryption in any form, RSA key generation, P-384,
ES384, RS384, RS512, PS384, PS512, ES256K, and JWE's `A*CBC-HS*` content encryption. A closed roster that
is only a habit reopens at the first ticket, so the list is written down. Unauthenticated and legacy
modes are out by [`core-api/tier-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-tier-roster); the size variants are out because two of everything
doubles the surface for no property a program can name; RSA encryption is out because RSA1_5 is a
padding oracle and RSA-OAEP buys nothing ECDH-ES does not, at a fraction of the key size.

**Where two algorithms take the same parameters they are one member with a closed enum argument**, the
way `Core\Hash::of` takes a `Core\Digest`; where the parameters differ they are separate members. **No
algorithm argument has a default** — not a cipher, not a digest, not a curve. A default is how a call
site copied from another file keeps an algorithm nobody re-read, and making the argument required buys a
`grep` that finds every use of a primitive on the day it has to be retired. The one member answering a
key with no algorithm in it, `generateKey()`, takes no algorithm argument at all: its 32 octets are the
single length both ciphers and every roster protocol share.

**AES-256-GCM is on the roster for interoperability and its sealed bytes say so**: `nonce(12) ‖
ciphertext ‖ tag(16)`, which is exactly what WebCrypto's `encrypt` answers with its IV put in front, so
a browser splits at byte 12 and does nothing else. XChaCha's stay `nonce(24) ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag(16)` and
remain the pair to prefer when both ends are Novis — advice on the member's reference card, never a
default. The nonce is drawn by the member and there is no nonce parameter, so AES-GCM carries its
birthday bound around 2^32 messages under one key; that bound is the price of reading what a browser
wrote, and the answer when a program approaches it is the other cipher rather than a counter the caller
keeps, which is a worse failure with a wider blast radius. Opening under the wrong cipher is a forgery,
never plausible bytes: both constructions authenticate before they decrypt, so a mismatched
`Crypto::Cipher` gets the same one `RuntimeError` sentence as every other message that is not authentic.

**A key is validated where it is read, not where it is used.** Every public key is checked at `read` — on
the curve for P-256, inside 2048–8192 bits for RSA — and an all-zero X25519 shared secret is refused at
`agree`, so there is no later site at which the check could be forgotten. An RSA key's scheme is fixed
when it is read, which is [`security/algorithm-comes-from-the-key`](security.md#security-algorithm-comes-from-the-key) held for the one key type two JWS
algorithms share. An RSA pair is never generated: `generateKeyPair` refuses both RSA kinds with a
`LogicError` naming `Crypto\KeyPair::read`, because a program is handed its RSA key by whoever issued
it. A key off the wire that fails is a `RuntimeError`; a malformed key the program built is a
`LogicError`. A JWK `read` accepts what a browser exports, `ext` and `key_ops` included, and refuses one
carrying `d`, because a private key handed over as a public one is a bug rather than an attack. A
private key leaves a `Crypto\KeyPair` only as `secret bytes` PKCS#8, and `Crypto\KeyPair::read` takes
DER or one PEM `PRIVATE KEY` block, the form a service-account file carries, and refuses PKCS#1 and
encrypted PKCS#8.

**PBKDF2's iteration count is required**, because the other end of an already-agreed protocol chose it
and a default would be a number that is either wrong or ignored. Its floor and ceiling are frozen in the
vector set as refusals, so neither number moves without that set being regenerated
([`security/jwe-compact-subset`](security.md#security-jwe-compact-subset) gives the bounds and why the ceiling matters).

The interop claim is checkable rather than intended: `bun nv webcrypto-vectors` freezes WebCrypto's
own output for every algorithm here, derived from labels so a rerun writes the same bytes. A suite
written against our own implementation proves only that our encoder and our decoder agree; the other
side's output is what proves interoperability.

- **Memory:** per call, a few hundred bytes of cipher or curve state on the stack and one output buffer
  charged to the request's budget before it is allocated. A `Crypto\KeyPair` holds its private scalar for
  as long as the program holds the object. Nothing is held between calls, so all of it is O(in-flight).

**Declined:**
- **A `string` algorithm argument, or one enum spanning every primitive.** One member taking any
  algorithm is how a program ends up with `aes-256-ecb` in one file. An enum is safer than a string but
  still lets `seal` be handed a signature algorithm; separate members where the parameters differ make
  that unrepresentable.
- **Defaulting the cipher to XChaCha20-Poly1305.** A default is invisible at the call site, and the call
  sites that matter are the interoperating ones, where the cipher is not ours to choose.
- **RSA-OAEP, for an issuer that encrypts ID tokens.** It is rare and opt-in at every provider, and it
  would bring RSA encryption's whole padding surface in for one feature.
- **JWK export of a private key, an additional-data parameter, and streaming encryption.** None is on the
  surface; JWE uses additional data internally, where the protocol fixes what it is.

<sub>See also [`core-api/tier-roster`](core-api.md#core-api-tier-roster), [`security/algorithm-comes-from-the-key`](security.md#security-algorithm-comes-from-the-key), [`security/jwe-compact-subset`](security.md#security-jwe-compact-subset), [`core-classes/secret-reveal`](core-classes.md#core-classes-secret-reveal).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-signature"></a>

## `Core\Signature` signs a canonicalized payload, and the lifetime rides inside the signed bytes

`rule:core-classes/signature`

`Core\Signature::sign` takes a map and an options bag carrying a key ring and a written lifetime, and
answers a token; `verify` takes a token and a key ring and answers the payload or throws.

**The input is a map, never text.** `sign` canonicalizes the payload itself — keys sorted, each value
encoded with its type — so there is no assembled string for the two sides to disagree about, which is
what every hand-rolled signing helper gets wrong. **The lifetime is inside the signed bytes**, not
beside them, so a holder cannot edit it and there is no second parameter to keep in step. The token
is URL-safe by construction — unpadded URL-safe base64 — so every octet is a legal cookie octet and a
legal query-string value and nothing downstream escapes it again. The key ring is newest-first:
signing uses the head, verifying tries the ring in order, rotating is prepending and retiring is
dropping the tail. It is the signed cookie's ring and shape, so there is one rotation vocabulary in
the language, not two.

**A verified payload is `tainted`.** A token minted by one service and read by another is not the
signed-cookie case, where the plaintext was the application's own when it went in; "we authored this
payload" is not a property the checker can see, so it is not one the return type may assume.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/router-signed-url`](core-classes.md#core-classes-router-signed-url), [`core-classes/uri-removable-components`](core-classes.md#core-classes-uri-removable-components), [`core-classes/secret-reveal`](core-classes.md#core-classes-secret-reveal).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony"></a>

## `Core\Passkey` creates WebAuthn options and verifies registration and sign-in for ES256 and Ed25519, with a single-use challenge, no attestation check, and the credential stored by the application

`rule:core-classes/passkey-verifies-a-webauthn-ceremony`

`Core\Passkey` creates the options for a WebAuthn registration or sign-in and verifies what the browser
returns, for ES256 and Ed25519 credentials, without verifying attestation, and the application stores
the credential it returns.

| Member | Does |
|---|---|
| `registerOptions(string $rpId, string $rpName, bytes $userId, string $userName, array<Passkey\Credential> $existing = []): string` | the JSON for `navigator.credentials.create()`, with a fresh challenge saved in the session |
| `verifyRegistration(tainted string $response, string $rpId, string $origin): Passkey\Credential` | checks the browser's answer and returns the new credential |
| `signInOptions(string $rpId, array<Passkey\Credential> $allowed = []): string` | the JSON for `navigator.credentials.get()`, with a fresh challenge saved in the session |
| `credentialId(tainted string $response): tainted bytes` | the credential id the browser claims, to look up the stored credential |
| `verifySignIn(tainted string $response, Passkey\Credential $stored, string $rpId, string $origin): Passkey\Credential` | checks the signature against the stored credential and returns it with its sign counter updated |

`Passkey\Credential` is a value with `id` (`bytes`), `publicKey` (`bytes`, the COSE key), `algorithm`
(`Passkey\Credential::Algorithm::ES256` or `Ed25519`) and `signCount` (`int`), each read by the
method of that name, and `Passkey\Credential::of($id, $publicKey, $algorithm, $signCount)` builds a
stored one again, checking the key against the algorithm. `Core\Passkey` reads and writes no
storage of its own: the application saves the credential wherever it keeps users.

**What verification checks:** the client data's type, challenge and origin; the authenticator data's
relying-party id hash, the user-present flag and the user-verified flag, which the options always ask
for; and, for a sign-in, the signature over both, verified by the code `Core\Crypto` already uses. A
credential whose algorithm is neither ES256 nor Ed25519 is refused at registration. A sign counter that
does not increase, when either value is not zero, throws.

**The challenge is single-use.** It comes from the system random source and is saved in the started
session ([`core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`](core-classes.md#core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly)). Verification takes it out of the session
before it checks anything, so a second verification of one challenge, a replayed response, throws.
The origin and relying-party id are the values the application passes, never anything the browser sent.

**What the browser sent is `tainted`**, and the credential a successful verification returns is not.
The CBOR and COSE parsing comes from an existing crate
([`packaging/somebody-elses-specification-is-a-crate`](packaging.md#packaging-somebody-elses-specification-is-a-crate)).

`Core\Passkey` is admitted to the protocol roster ([`security/protocol-roster`](security.md#security-protocol-roster)). Its usual failure
is a silent library bug — an unchecked origin, a skipped flag, a challenge accepted twice returns a
signed-in user — and every web application that signs people in needs it. The registry signs owners
in with it ([`packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`](packaging.md#packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey)).

**Memory:** one challenge per ceremony, in the session, until it is verified.

**Declined:**
- **Attestation verification.** It needs a vendor certificate list that changes over time, and a
  registry or web application has no use for knowing the authenticator's maker.
- **Every COSE algorithm.** ES256 and Ed25519 cover current authenticators, and each further algorithm
  is more parsing to get wrong.
- **Credential storage inside `Core`.** Where users are kept is the application's choice, and a `Core`
  table would be a second user store beside it.
- **A challenge the application creates and passes back in.** Nothing could then stop one challenge
  from verifying twice.

<sub>See also [`security/protocol-roster`](security.md#security-protocol-roster), [`security/protocol-admission-test`](security.md#security-protocol-admission-test), [`core-classes/session-is-started-explicitly`](core-classes.md#core-classes-session-is-started-explicitly), [`packaging/somebody-elses-specification-is-a-crate`](packaging.md#packaging-somebody-elses-specification-is-a-crate), [`packaging/a-registry-account-is-a-passkey`](packaging.md#packaging-a-registry-account-is-a-passkey).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message"></a>

## `Core\WebPush::send` encrypts a payload as RFC 8291 `aes128gcm` with the nonce derived inside, signs a VAPID token, and sends under `net.connect`

`rule:core-classes/web-push-sends-an-encrypted-message`

`Core\WebPush::send` encrypts one payload for a browser's push subscription as RFC 8291's `aes128gcm`
encoding, with the nonce derived inside and never a parameter, signs a VAPID token with the
application's P-256 key as RFC 8292 says, and sends the message through `Core`'s HTTP client under the
ordinary `net.connect` grant.

| Member | Does |
|---|---|
| `subscription(tainted string $json): WebPush\Subscription` | reads the browser's `PushSubscription.toJSON()`: the endpoint URL and its `p256dh` and `auth` values |
| `applicationServerKey(Crypto\KeyPair $vapid): string` | the public key, base64url, that the browser's `pushManager.subscribe()` needs |
| `send(WebPush\Subscription $to, bytes $payload, Crypto\KeyPair $vapid, string $subject, int $ttl = 86400): WebPush\Sent` | encrypts, signs and sends one message, and returns the push service's answer |

`WebPush\Sent` has the push service's `status` and `gone`, which is `true` for a subscription the
service no longer knows, so the application can drop it. The VAPID key is a `Core\Crypto\KeyPair` of
kind `P256` and stays `secret`; it never appears in a message or an error. The token is signed by the
code `Core\Jwt` already uses for ES256.

**The encryption is fixed.** Each message draws a fresh salt and a fresh P-256 key pair from the system
random source, agrees a secret with the subscription's `p256dh`, and derives the content key and the
nonce with HKDF and the `auth` secret, as RFC 8291 says. A payload larger than one record, 3993 bytes,
throws. A `p256dh` value not on the curve, an `auth` value of the wrong length and an endpoint that is
not `https:` each throw.

**AES-128-GCM is internal to `Core\WebPush`.** No `Core` cipher takes a caller-chosen nonce, and this
class adds none: AES-128-GCM is not a new case of `Core\Crypto\Cipher`, so the cipher roster of
[`core-classes/crypto-interop-tier`](core-classes.md#core-classes-crypto-interop-tier) does not change.

**The endpoint came from a browser, so it is `tainted`**, and the HTTP client's outbound address table
refuses an internal host for it as for any request ([`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy)). A subscription
cannot make the server reach its own network.

`Core\WebPush` is admitted to the protocol roster ([`security/protocol-roster`](security.md#security-protocol-roster)). Its usual failure is
a silent library bug — a reused nonce or a wrong key derivation still produces bytes that look
encrypted — and a web application that notifies its users needs it. The registry notifies owners with
it ([`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email)).

**Memory:** one encrypted message per call, freed when `send` returns.

**Declined:**
- **AES-128-GCM as a public cipher in `Core\Crypto`.** Its only caller needs a nonce derived by the
  protocol, and a public cipher would need a caller-chosen one.
- **A caller-chosen nonce, salt or record size.** Each is a way to break the encryption, and RFC 8291
  fixes all three.
- **Encryption only, with the sending left to the application.** The application would then build the
  VAPID header itself, which is the part most often wrong.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/crypto-interop-tier`](core-classes.md#core-classes-crypto-interop-tier), [`security/protocol-roster`](security.md#security-protocol-roster), [`security/protocol-admission-test`](security.md#security-protocol-admission-test), [`security/net-address-policy`](security.md#security-net-address-policy), [`packaging/an-owner-is-notified-without-email`](packaging.md#packaging-an-owner-is-notified-without-email).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-router-signed-url"></a>

## `Core\Router` signs a route's path pattern and its parameters, so a signature survives a remount and a method rename

`rule:core-classes/router-signed-url`

`Core\Router` keeps its own signing pair — `urlSigned`, which mints a signed URL from a route's method
reference and its typed parameters, and `signedRoute`, which verifies against the match the server
already made and answers that `Router\Match` or throws. Parsing a built URL and signing it would reach
most of this, and convenience alone would not justify two more members.

**One property does.** A compiled route table may be served at one mount prefix or another, so a
signed *URL* stops verifying the moment a mount moves. `urlSigned` signs the route's **path pattern**
— the mount-relative `#[Route]` `path`, such as `/unsubscribe/{reader}` — and its parameter values,
and verification reads the existing match rather than re-parsing anything. A remount and a rename of
the handler method leave old links valid. A changed path breaks them, which a changed URL does anyway.

**Verification is the application's, called by hand, wherever it keeps it.** Nothing verifies a
signature for you, because the program that renders the refusal is the program that should decide
when to ask.

**Declined:**
- **Signing the handler's `Class::method`.** A refactor that renames a method would invalidate every
  link already sent, such as an unsubscribe link in a mail, with no change to the URL a reader sees.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/signature`](core-classes.md#core-classes-signature).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-uri-removable-components"></a>

## `Core\Uri` spends the omitted-versus-null distinction on three components and on one query parameter at a time

`rule:core-classes/uri-removable-components`

Three of a URI's components become nullable — `port`, `query` and `fragment` — and writing `null` for
one in a `with` bag **removes** it, where omitting the key leaves it alone. The other three stay
non-nullable, because in each case what looks like a removal is a different operation wearing its
clothes: every reference has a path, and an empty one is `""`; clearing a host would silently clear
the port and user-info a caller did not mention, which is a cascade rather than a removal; and
dropping a scheme turns an absolute URI into a relative reference, which is a member's worth of
behaviour rather than a field's. A removal still goes through the same recompose-and-reread path
every other `with` takes, so a component that would move is the same throw a bad replacement already
is.

**A query parameter is the second level.** A URI's components are fixed and few; its parameters are
dynamic and many, and replacing the whole query string is what makes every call site parse, edit and
rebuild — which is where this area's two real bugs come from. A singular reader and a singular writer
close it, composing the three existing members so no second canonicalization exists to drift. A
`null` value removes the parameter, the bracket convention comes free because a value may itself be
an array, and removing the last parameter leaves no query at all rather than a bare `?`.

`crates/nvs-stdlib/src/uri.rs` is where both levels are: `with` takes `port`, `query` and `fragment`
as `?T` and its `removable` helper reads the three states, and `queryParameter` and
`withQueryParameter` compose that module's own `query` slot, `parse_query` and `build` so that the
query string gains no second canonicalization. The name a parameter is reached by is **top-level**,
so an array value is what writes brackets — which is what makes the pair a round trip rather than
two members that each invented a spelling.

The pair is singular and reached by name, the same operation `Core\Request::query(string $name)` performs
on the same bracket convention from the other side of a request. A query keeps exactly one syntax per
state: pairs are written by this pair, an empty query is `with({query: ""})`, and no query is
`with({query: null})`. There is no plural `withQueryParameters` and no `withoutQueryParameter`: setting
several is the member twice or the existing parse-and-build pair, and removing is `null`.

`userInfo` is not a key of the `with` bag at all, so `with` neither adds nor drops a credential.

**Declined:**
- **One member per removable component, such as `withoutFragment()`.** It multiplies the surface by the
  number of clearable components on every class that has any. Symmetric naming
  ([`core-api/symmetric-names`](core-api.md#core-api-symmetric-names)) would then want `with` and `without` treated as a pair, which they
  are not: one takes an anonymous object and the other would take names.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/signature`](core-classes.md#core-classes-signature).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-output-that-scales-with-its-input-bounds-the-input"></a>

## A member whose output scales with its input either allocates through the guarded value allocator or bounds the input

`rule:core-classes/output-that-scales-with-its-input-bounds-the-input`

A `Core` member whose output scales with its input takes one of exactly two obligations: it allocates
that output through the value allocator the memory ceiling guards, or it bounds the input it accepts.
There is no third option, and a member that took neither is how a request holds many times its own
`[limits] memory` in one call. The obligation is general rather than one member's paragraph because
the residual is a small format factor for the members that ship and a thousandfold one for the first
member with a large expansion ratio; stating it before that member exists is cheaper than finding
which members quietly took neither branch.

The ceiling is asked in front of a value allocation, so a member that grows a Novis `string` or
`array` as it goes is bounded by construction: the first allocation past the ceiling is refused and
the request is stopped. What escapes it is a member that assembles its result in its own buffer and
hands the finished thing over at the end — the ceiling is then asked once, after the bytes were
already held, and the residual is the member's whole expansion ratio.

So a member with an expansion ratio bounds the input instead, and the two shipped instances are the
shape to copy. [`core-classes/regex-two-tiers`](core-classes.md#core-classes-regex-two-tiers) bounds a backtracking search by steps rather than
by the size of what it produces. [`core-classes/decompression-bound`](core-classes.md#core-classes-decompression-bound) bounds a decode by
`min(input × ratio, ceiling)`, applies it while the output grows rather than to a buffer already
allocated, and refuses rather than truncating.

A bound written this way is part of the member's contract: it is stated in the member's own rule, the
breach it raises is named there, and a caller may lower it and never raise it. A member that instead
takes the first branch says so — its result is built through the value allocator and it holds no
buffer of its own that the ceiling has not seen.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/decompression-bound`](core-classes.md#core-classes-decompression-bound), [`core-classes/regex-two-tiers`](core-classes.md#core-classes-regex-two-tiers), [`errors/an-allocation-past-the-ceiling-is-refused-in-front-of-itself`](errors.md#errors-an-allocation-past-the-ceiling-is-refused-in-front-of-itself).</sub>

<a id="core-classes-decompression-bound"></a>

## Every decompression runs under an output ceiling and a ratio, and there is no spelling for turning either off

`rule:core-classes/decompression-bound`

Every decompression runs under an absolute output ceiling and a ratio of output to input, and a
call may lower either and raise neither. The two are one bound: an absolute ceiling alone is one
every request may reach whatever it sent, and a ratio alone lets a large input buy a proportionately
large output, so what a decode compares against is `min(input × ratio, ceiling)`.

`[limits] max_decompressed` and `[limits] max_decompression_ratio` carry the ceiling, default to
64 MiB and 1000:1, and are `System`-class — an operator's decision, never a request's. A call names
`$maxBytes` and `$maxRatio` to ask for less, and gets the smaller of the ask and the configured
value on each axis independently. 64 MiB is far above any document a request decompresses, such as
a JSON body, an HTML page, a spreadsheet or a CSV export, and below what a request may hold under the
default `[limits] memory`, so a breach is an error the request survives. 1000:1 is above every input
